nameStory: The black maple gets its name from its distinctively dark, deeply grooved bark that appears almost charcoal-black compared to other maples. This darker appearance sets it apart from its close cousin, the sugar maple, which has lighter gray bark with shallower furrows.
description: Black maple is a large deciduous tree that can grow 60-80 feet tall with a rounded crown. It looks very similar to sugar maple and is sometimes considered the same species by botanists. The tree has the classic maple shape with opposite branches and produces the familiar winged seeds that helicopter down in fall. Black maples are much less common than sugar maples in New England, making them an exciting find for tree enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Look for leaves with typically three main lobes (occasionally five) that have a distinctive drooping appearance, like they're gently wilting. The undersides feel soft and fuzzy to the touch, and the leaf stems (petioles) are noticeably thick and sturdy.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: The bark is darker and more deeply furrowed than sugar maple, with a charcoal-black to dark gray color. Run your hand along it - the grooves feel deeper and more pronounced than other maples.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The winged seeds (samaras) are slightly smaller than sugar maple seeds but still helicopter down in classic maple fashion. They appear in pairs joined at the base.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a large, rounded crown similar to sugar maple but often appears less symmetrical. The overall silhouette is stately and broad when mature.

habitat: Black maple prefers rich, moist soils in mixed hardwood forests, often alongside sugar maple, American beech, and yellow birch. In New England, it's found in scattered locations, typically in river valleys and lower slopes where soils stay consistently moist. It's much rarer than sugar maple and tends to occur in small, isolated populations.

seasonality.spring: Small yellowish-green flowers appear with the emerging leaves in April to May. New leaves unfurl with their characteristic droopy appearance and fuzzy undersides.
seasonality.summer: The three-lobed, drooping leaves are at their most distinctive, with the soft, downy undersides clearly visible when wind flips them over.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant yellow to orange, similar to sugar maple. The winged seeds mature and begin their spinning descent to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Identify by the distinctively dark, deeply grooved bark and sturdy branching pattern. Buds are similar to sugar maple - brown and pointed.

funFact: Black maple and sugar maple hybridize so frequently that some scientists consider them the same species - making every black maple potentially part of a massive, ongoing evolutionary romance story spanning thousands of years.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sugar maple, which typically has five-lobed leaves that stand upright rather than droop. Memory trick: 'Black maple leaves look sad and droopy with three lobes, sugar maple leaves look perky with five.' Also check the bark - black maple's is much darker and more deeply grooved.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific debate continues over whether black maple is its own species (Acer nigrum) or just a variety of sugar maple (Acer saccharum subsp. nigrum). This taxonomic uncertainty reflects how closely related and frequently hybridized these trees are, making field identification both challenging and scientifically significant.
compareHints: Black maple differs from sugar maple by having typically three-lobed (vs. five-lobed) drooping leaves with fuzzy undersides, darker and more deeply grooved bark, and slightly smaller seeds. Red maple has three-lobed leaves too, but they're not droopy, have whitish undersides, and red maple has smooth gray bark with red twigs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
Unlike our common native maples with their distinctly lobed leaves, Tatarian maple often has simple, oval leaves with just shallow lobes or none at all.
